scenes.title: TRIGGER IS NOT THE FILL
scenes.overlay: A stop level is not a fill.
scenes.narration: A trailing stop can trigger and still fill at a different price. The trigger is a condition, not a promise.

scenes.title: TRACKS A NEW HIGH
scenes.narration: A sell trailing stop tracks the highest price reached after the order is accepted. The trail is set as a percentage or a dollar amount below that high-water mark. When the market makes a new high, the stop can move upward with it. The reference is the high-water mark, not your original entry.

scenes.title: DOES NOT LOOSEN
scenes.overlay: It does not follow price down.
scenes.narration: If price falls, the stop level does not move back down. It stays at its last higher level while the market reverses. A small pullback may leave the order waiting; a larger move may reach the trigger. The order reacts to its rule. It does not predict the next move.

scenes.title: MARKET ORDER. NOT A PROMISE.
scenes.narration: When the trigger is reached, the stop becomes a market order. A market order seeks available liquidity, not a guaranteed price. In a fast move, a price gap, or a trading halt, the next available fill can be worse than the trigger. The stop level is not an execution promise.

scenes.title: REGULAR HOURS MATTER
scenes.narration: Broker rules matter. Alpaca says trailing stops do not trigger outside regular market hours. An overnight gap can happen before the order is eligible again. A good-till-canceled order may persist across sessions, but it is not an around-the-clock safety net.

scenes.title: KNOW THE LIMITS
scenes.narration: Before relying on any stop, learn how your broker defines the trigger. Check whether it uses trades or quotes, when it can trigger, and what happens after a halt. A trailing stop is an order-management tool, not a guaranteed maximum loss or profit lock. It does not replace checking order status. What rule would you verify first?
